overall_summary: The channel's performance is heavily driven by extreme space anomalies and bizarre planetary phenomena, which consistently capture the highest views and engagement. Conversely, psychology, brain facts, and self-help-style content struggle to gain traction, indicating a clear audience preference for cosmic wonder over human biology.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice Will Break Your Brain!' achieved 1,054 views, and 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b' reached 909 views with high relative engagement (34 likes, 2 comments). 'The Largest Ocean in Space' also performed strongly with 460 views.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on extreme cosmic environments, focusing on mind-bending physics, terrifying planetary conditions, and cosmic scale comparisons.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (52 views), 'Your Brain Is Hiding This From You' (38 views), and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) consistently underperformed.
weak_patterns.action: Pivot away from standard cognitive science facts unless they can be framed through a highly dramatic, cinematic mystery lens.

next_video.hook_style: Visual paradox with high-stakes cosmic doom
next_video.concept: The planet that is literally being eaten alive by its own star (WASP-12b).
next_video.opening_direction: Start with a dramatic, high-contrast visual of an egg-shaped planet stretching toward a massive star. Voiceover: 'Right now, there is a planet in our galaxy that is literally being eaten alive.'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the star's gravity is so intense it has distorted the planet into a football shape, and it is devouring 189 quadrillion tons of its mass every single year.
next_video.reason: Leverages the proven success of extreme planetary anomalies (like TrES-2b and Gliese 436b) while utilizing a highly visual, high-stakes hook to maximize early retention.

experiment: Test a 'Cinematic Space Survival' narrative style for cosmic anomalies, shifting from a list of facts to a dramatic, second-person perspective ('If you stood on this planet, you would...') to see if it boosts average view duration.
